title.en: What is DevOps? Start with a food-order app.

concept.en: Imagine you own a food-order app. Customers tap a button to order lunch. Someone must build that button, and someone must keep it working. Today, you will understand how those people work together. No coding or installation today.

lessons.analogy: A restaurant needs a cook to prepare food and a team to serve customers. Good cooking alone is not enough if nobody can receive an order. An app also needs people who build it and people who keep it available.

steps.title: An app follows instructions
steps.text: You tap Place order. The computer follows instructions written by a person and shows Order received. Those instructions are called software. The screen you see is only one part of the app.
steps.example: Our example app currently charges ₹100 for lunch. Tap the customer button to see what a customer receives.
steps.meaning: Instructions that tell a computer what to do.

steps.title: A developer changes it
steps.text: You decide to offer a ₹10 discount. A developer changes the app instructions so lunch can cost ₹90. A developer is a person who writes or changes software. Saving this change does not automatically change what customers are using.
steps.example: The developer has prepared the discount. Our example customer still sees ₹100 because the changed app has not been made available yet.
steps.meaning: A person who writes or changes the instructions of an app.

steps.title: Operations makes it available
steps.text: The change is checked, then the updated app is made available to customers. The operations team helps the app run and stay available. Now a customer can use the discount and pay ₹90. You will learn the technical steps on later days.
steps.example: The updated example is now available. Tap the customer button: the price has changed from ₹100 to ₹90.
steps.meaning: The work of running an app and keeping it available for people.

steps.title: They keep working together
steps.text: After the update, the team checks whether customers can still order. If something breaks, they investigate and fix it together. DevOps is a way for development and operations to share this responsibility and improve how changes reach users. It is not the name of one tool.
steps.example: The discount is useful only if customers can still place an order. Building, checking, making available and looking after the app belong to one shared journey.
steps.meaning: A way for development and operations to work together to deliver and run software.

lessons.commands:
No terminal or commands today.
1. Read the four short parts.
2. Try the example customer button in each part.
3. Explain the roles in your own words.

expected.en: You can explain three things without reading: the developer changes the app; operations helps run it; DevOps helps them work together. You do not need to memorize any tool names.

challenge.en: Imagine the discount appears but the order button stops working. Who should help? Explain why the people building the app and the people running it should investigate together.

quiz.question: After an app update, customers cannot order. What is the DevOps approach?
options: The people building and running the app investigate together
Install more tools without checking the problem
quiz.explanation: They share responsibility for the customer experience. Tools can help later, but teamwork and clear feedback come first.

lessons.goal: Explain what a developer does, what operations does, and why they work together.
lessons.prerequisite: Nothing to install. You only need to know what it means to use an app.
lessons.takeaway: DevOps connects the people who build software with the people who run it.

glossary.meaning: Instructions that tell a computer what to do.
A person who writes or changes the instructions of an app.
The work of running an app and keeping it available for people.
A way for development and operations to work together to deliver and run software.

title.en: Meet files, folders and the terminal

concept.en: An app is stored in files on a computer. Folders keep those files together. A terminal is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking buttons. Today, learn these three ideas before installing development tools.

lessons.analogy: A file is like one sheet of paper. A folder is like a file holder. The terminal is another way to ask your computer to show or work with those items.

steps.title: Find a file
steps.text: Open your normal file manager: File Explorer on Windows or Finder on macOS. A photo or text document is a file. Its name helps you identify it. You do not need an app project yet.
steps.example: Find one document you already know. Notice its name and the folder containing it.
steps.meaning: One saved item on a computer, such as a document, photo or program.

steps.title: Make a learning folder
steps.text: Create a new folder called DevOps-Learning in a location you can find again. A folder groups related files. This is your practice space; do not use a work project or confidential folder.
steps.example: You can open DevOps-Learning and explain where it is saved.
steps.meaning: A place that groups files and other folders.

steps.title: Open a terminal
steps.text: On Windows, open PowerShell from the Start menu. On macOS, open Terminal. On Linux, open your terminal app. Opening this window does not change your files. You will type only a simple display command today.
steps.example: The window shows a place where you can type. That is the prompt.
steps.meaning: A window where you can type commands for your computer to carry out.

steps.title: Ask where you are
steps.text: Type pwd and press Enter. It prints the current folder location in PowerShell, macOS Terminal or a typical Linux shell. This command asks a question; it does not delete or edit anything.
steps.example: Read the printed location. It may be your home folder rather than DevOps-Learning. That is normal.
steps.meaning: An instruction you type and run by pressing Enter.

lessons.commands: pwd

expected.en: You found a file, created a practice folder, opened a terminal and read the folder location printed by pwd. These are four separate actions; take them one at a time.

challenge.en: Compare clicking a folder in the file manager with looking at the terminal location. They do not automatically move together. Explain why you must know which folder the terminal is using.

quiz.question: What is a terminal?
quiz.explanation: A terminal lets you ask the computer to do something by typing a command.

lessons.goal: Find a file, make a practice folder and run your first harmless command.
lessons.prerequisite: Day 1. A Windows, macOS or Linux computer. No Git or Python required.
lessons.tools: Your file manager and built-in terminal
lessons.takeaway: Files store things, folders organize them, and a terminal accepts typed commands.

glossary.meaning: One saved item on a computer, such as a document, photo or program.
A place that groups files and other folders.
A window where you can type commands for your computer to carry out.
An instruction you type and run by pressing Enter.

concept.en: Python is a language people use to write instructions for a computer. You do not need to learn the whole language today. Install it from the official source, check that it starts, and ask it to print one sentence.

lessons.analogy: A recipe gives instructions to a cook. A Python program gives instructions to a computer. Today you will write just one instruction.

steps.title: Know what Python is
steps.text: Different human languages express ideas. Programming languages express instructions for computers. Python is one of them. In this course it runs our small practice app.
steps.example: The instruction print("Hello") tells Python to display Hello.
steps.meaning: A way to write instructions that a computer can follow.

steps.title: Install it carefully
steps.text: Use the official Python downloads page linked in the activity below. Choose a supported Python 3 version, 3.11 or newer. On Windows, use the installer option to add Python to PATH if offered. Close and reopen your terminal afterward.
steps.example: PATH is a list of places your computer searches when you type a program name.
steps.meaning: Put a program on your computer so you can run it.

steps.title: Check the version
steps.text: Type python --version. If Windows cannot find it, try py --version. On macOS or Linux, try python3 --version. Use whichever command successfully reports Python 3.11 or newer in later commands.
steps.example: Python 3.12.x is one acceptable result. The last number can differ.
steps.meaning: A number that identifies a particular edition of a program.

steps.title: Print a sentence
steps.text: Run the one-line example in the activity. The -c option means run the instructions inside the quotes. print displays a message. This creates no cloud service and needs no account.
steps.example: The output should be Hello, I am learning DevOps. Your computer just followed your first Python instruction.
steps.meaning: The result a program displays or produces.

lessons.commands:
python --version
python -c "print('Hello, I am learning DevOps')"

expected.en: The first command shows Python 3.11 or newer. The second prints Hello, I am learning DevOps. If you used py or python3 for the first command, use that same name for the second.

challenge.en: Change only the sentence inside the quotes and run it again. Then leave out a closing quote once, read the error, and restore it. An error is feedback about the instruction, not a reason to reinstall everything.

quiz.question: What does print do in our tiny example?
quiz.explanation: print asks Python to display the supplied message.

lessons.goal: Run one Python instruction and explain the output.
lessons.prerequisite: Day 2: you can open a terminal. Download Python only from python.org.
lessons.takeaway: A program is a set of instructions. You can run one small instruction and inspect its result.

glossary.meaning: A way to write instructions that a computer can follow.
Put a program on your computer so you can run it.
A number that identifies a particular edition of a program.
The result a program displays or produces.

concept.en: Start a program, make one request and stop the program you started. Start with the short explanation below. Read the new-word meaning, follow one part at a time, and try the activity only when the idea makes sense. You do not need to memorize a list of tool names.

lessons.analogy: A recipe is not a running kitchen. A process is the kitchen at work; a port is a service counter.

steps.title: Start
steps.text: A program is a saved set of instructions. A process is that program while it is running. Extract the sample project ZIP, open its folder, then open a terminal in that folder. Run python app.py. Use py or python3 if that was your working Python command on Day 3.
steps.meaning: A program while it is running.
steps.example: A recipe is not a running kitchen. A process is the kitchen at work; a port is a service counter.

steps.title: Request
steps.text: While the program is running, open http://localhost:8000/health in your browser. The program answers the browser request. A program that answers other programs is acting as a server. localhost means your own computer.
steps.meaning: A program or computer that answers requests from other programs.
steps.example: Open localhost:8000/health in a browser or a second terminal.

steps.title: Understand the port
steps.text: The number 8000 is a port: a numbered connection point for the program. Keep the default today. Later you can stop the app, change its port, and use the new number in the browser URL.
steps.meaning: A numbered connection point used to reach a program.
steps.example: Stop with Ctrl+C. In Bash run PORT=8001 python app.py, then use localhost:8001.

steps.title: Stop
steps.text: Click the terminal running your app and press Ctrl+C. This asks your foreground program to stop. Refresh the browser. The app cannot answer now because its process has stopped. Start it again to restore the response.
steps.meaning: A keyboard shortcut that asks the foreground program to stop.
steps.example: Use Ctrl+C on your own foreground service and verify requests stop working.

lessons.commands: python app.py

expected.en: Your browser shows {"status": "ok"} while the program runs. After Ctrl+C, refreshing the page fails. Starting the app again restores the response. These observations explain why instructions saved on disk are different from a running process.

challenge.en: Start a second copy on port 8000. Diagnose Address already in use, then stop only the extra process you started.

quiz.question: Why can a second app fail to start?
quiz.explanation: An existing listener can prevent another bind to the same port.

glossary.meaning: A program while it is running.
A program or computer that answers requests from other programs.
A numbered connection point used to reach a program.
A keyboard shortcut that asks the foreground program to stop.

lessons.goal: Start a program, make one request and stop the program you started.
lessons.prerequisite: Day 3: Python works. Download the sample project ZIP using the link in this activity, extract it, and open a terminal in the extracted folder.
lessons.tools: Python and the downloaded sample project
lessons.takeaway: Start a program, make one request and stop the program you started.
lessons.overview: A program on disk becomes a process when it runs. The process listens on a port so other programs can connect. Environment variables provide runtime configuration. Two processes usually cannot bind the same address and port at once. A stopped process cannot answer requests even if its source files still exist.

title.en: Exit codes, logs and safe shell habits

concept.en: Programs can show messages and can also return a result number. That number helps another program decide whether the work succeeded. Today you will compare one successful instruction with one deliberate failure. You do not need Docker, Git or tests yet.

lessons.analogy: An alarm that prints a warning but reports everything is fine cannot protect a building.

steps.title: Display a normal message
steps.text: Run the first print command in the activity. Python displays Starting my practice. This visible message is output. A program can print several messages as it works.
steps.example: A message saying Starting does not prove that the rest of the program finished.
steps.meaning: Something a program displays or produces.

steps.title: Ask whether it finished successfully
steps.text: Immediately after that command, inspect the exit code. In PowerShell type $LASTEXITCODE. In Bash or macOS Terminal type echo $?. A successful run usually returns 0.
steps.example: Read the result number separately from the sentence printed by the program.
steps.meaning: A number returned when a program finishes. Zero usually means success.

steps.title: Create a harmless failure
steps.text: Run the second Python command, which deliberately exits with code 7. It changes no files. Inspect the exit code immediately afterward using the command for your terminal.
steps.example: The result is 7 instead of 0. Another program can use that number to know the work failed.
steps.meaning: Any number other than zero; commonly used to signal failure.

steps.title: Read the message and the result
steps.text: A printed message helps a person understand an event. An exit code helps automation decide what to do next. Look at both. Later, you will use recorded messages, called logs, to investigate problems.
steps.example: A script that prints All good but returns a failure code needs investigation. A message and a result number are different evidence.
steps.meaning: A recorded message about something a program did.

lessons.commands:
python -c "print('Starting my practice')"
# Now inspect the exit code:
# PowerShell: $LASTEXITCODE
# Bash/macOS Terminal: echo $?

python -c "raise SystemExit(7)"
# Inspect the exit code again using your terminal’s command.

expected.en: The print command returns 0. The deliberate SystemExit command returns 7. You can explain why displaying a sentence and finishing successfully are different things.

challenge.en: Replace 7 with 3 in the deliberate exit command. Predict the next result number before running it. This is a controlled local exercise; you are not breaking your computer.

quiz.question: What should a failed verification return?
quiz.explanation: Automation needs a machine-readable failure signal.

glossary.meaning: A number a program returns when it finishes. Zero usually means success.
A recorded message describing something a program did.
The normal output channel of a program.
The output channel commonly used for errors.

lessons.goal: Read a result and explain how a command signals success or failure.
lessons.prerequisite: Day 3: you can run Python. Use py or python3 if that is your working command. No sample project or Docker required.
lessons.takeaway: Read a result and explain how a command signals success or failure.
lessons.overview: Automation cannot rely on a person noticing a red line. Programs return exit codes: zero conventionally means success, nonzero means failure. stdout and stderr carry output, but a message that says success is not the same as an actual successful exit. Shell pipelines need deliberate error handling.

concept.en: Record one small change with Git. Start with the short explanation below. Read the new-word meaning, follow one part at a time, and try the activity only when the idea makes sense. You do not need to memorize a list of tool names.

lessons.analogy: A saved notebook entry is different from sending that notebook to your team.

steps.title: Inspect
steps.text: Run git status to see the current branch and changed files.
steps.meaning: A tool that records changes to project files.
steps.example: A saved notebook entry is different from sending that notebook to your team.

steps.title: Branch
steps.text: Create a learning branch rather than modifying main directly.
steps.meaning: One recorded snapshot of your changes.
steps.example: Create a learning branch rather than modifying main directly.

steps.title: Change
steps.text: Make one small documentation correction and inspect git diff.
steps.meaning: A separate line of work that keeps a proposed change apart from main.
steps.example: Make one small documentation correction and inspect git diff.

steps.title: Record
steps.text: Stage that file, commit with a useful message, then inspect the new commit.
steps.meaning: A separate line of work that keeps a proposed change apart from main.
steps.example: Stage that file, commit with a useful message, then inspect the new commit.

lessons.commands:
git --version
git clone https://github.com/svrforge/devops-first-pipeline.git
cd devops-first-pipeline
git status
git switch -c learning/day-06
# After editing START-HERE.md:
git diff
git add START-HERE.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Clarify local setup instructions"

expected.en: You can explain which file changed and see it in one local commit. If Git asks for your identity, configure it using the official Git setup guide, then try again. A local commit is not yet uploaded to GitHub.

challenge.en: Edit two files but stage only one. Inspect git diff and git diff --staged to understand the difference.

quiz.question: What does staging select?
options: The changes to include in the next commit
quiz.explanation: The index defines the content of the next commit.

glossary.meaning: A tool that records changes to project files.
One recorded snapshot of your changes.
A separate line of work that keeps a proposed change apart from main.

lessons.goal: Record one small change with Git.
lessons.prerequisite: Install Git from the official guide. A commit also needs a Git name/email configured. Use a separate copy of this learning project, not a work repository.
lessons.takeaway: Record one small change with Git.
lessons.overview: Git records snapshots, not just filenames. A commit should explain one coherent change. Inspect your working tree and diff before staging. Staging specific files helps avoid publishing unrelated notes or credentials. A local commit has not automatically reached GitHub.

concept.en: Explain how a pull request helps people check a change before sharing it. Start with the short explanation below. Read the new-word meaning, follow one part at a time, and try the activity only when the idea makes sense. You do not need to memorize a list of tool names.

lessons.analogy: A quality gate should check the actual parcel before it enters the delivery route.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.text: Visitors should fork and clone their own copy before pushing.
steps.meaning: A project folder and its recorded change history.
steps.example: A quality gate should check the actual parcel before it enters the delivery route.

steps.title: Push
steps.text: Push a feature branch to a repository where you have permission.
steps.meaning: A proposal to bring changes from one branch into another.
steps.example: Push a feature branch to a repository where you have permission.

steps.title: Review
steps.text: Open a PR and read the diff, not only the title. Identify the tested commit SHA.
steps.meaning: An automated result that helps decide whether a change can be merged.
steps.example: Open a PR and read the diff, not only the title. Identify the tested commit SHA.

steps.title: Merge
steps.text: Wait for all required checks and resolve conversations. Do not bypass the gate.
steps.meaning: An automated result that helps decide whether a change can be merged.
steps.example: Wait for all required checks and resolve conversations. Do not bypass the gate.

lessons.commands:
git status
git push -u origin learning/day-06

expected.en: A PR shows the intended diff and check results for its latest commit. Forks need their own protection settings.

challenge.en: Push a deliberate failing test on a disposable branch, observe the red check, fix it, and verify the newer commit passes.

quiz.question: Should main receive an unverified direct push?
options: No, use the protected PR flow
Yes, if the title looks good
quiz.explanation: The PR flow keeps verification connected to proposed changes.

glossary.meaning: A project folder and its recorded change history.
A proposal to bring changes from one branch into another.
An automated result that helps decide whether a change can be merged.

lessons.goal: Explain how a pull request helps people check a change before sharing it.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete Day 6 first. If its activity is unclear, go back before adding a new tool.
lessons.takeaway: Explain how a pull request helps people check a change before sharing it.
lessons.overview: A branch is a separate line of work. A pull request proposes bringing that work into another branch and makes checks and discussion visible. Protection on main requires the configured checks and an up-to-date branch. It prevents known failing changes from merging; it cannot prove every possible behavior is correct.

concept.en: Tell the difference between a connection failure and a missing web page. Start with the short explanation below. Read the new-word meaning, follow one part at a time, and try the activity only when the idea makes sense. You do not need to memorize a list of tool names.

lessons.analogy: Reaching the shop door is different from finding the product you asked for.

steps.title: Address
steps.text: The URL names a destination and optional port.
steps.meaning: The program asking for something, such as your browser.
steps.example: Reaching the shop door is different from finding the product you asked for.

steps.title: Connect
steps.text: The client tries to connect to a process listening at that address.
steps.meaning: Rules a browser and a web server use to exchange requests and responses.
steps.example: The client tries to connect to a process listening at that address.

steps.title: Request
steps.text: The client sends a method and path such as GET /health.
steps.meaning: A response number: 200 means success here; 404 means the requested route was not found.
steps.example: The client sends a method and path such as GET /health.

steps.title: Respond
steps.text: The server returns status, headers and a body. Inspect all three when debugging.
steps.meaning: A response number: 200 means success here; 404 means the requested route was not found.
steps.example: The server returns status, headers and a body. Inspect all three when debugging.

lessons.commands:
python app.py
# In a second terminal with curl:
curl -i http://localhost:8000/health

expected.en: The response is HTTP 200 with JSON content type and status ok. The server logs the request.

challenge.en: Call port 8001 while the app listens on 8000, then call /missing on 8000. Explain refused connection versus 404.

quiz.question: Where does a 404 come from?
quiz.explanation: A 404 is an application response for a resource not found.

glossary.meaning: The program asking for something, such as your browser.
Rules a browser and a web server use to exchange requests and responses.
A response number: 200 means success here; 404 means the requested route was not found.

lessons.goal: Tell the difference between a connection failure and a missing web page.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete Day 7 first. If its activity is unclear, go back before adding a new tool.
lessons.takeaway: Tell the difference between a connection failure and a missing web page.
lessons.overview: A browser request involves name lookup, a network connection and an application response. localhost refers to the machine making the request. The port selects a listening service. HTTP status describes the application result after a connection exists. Connection refused and HTTP 404 are different layers of failure.

concept.en: Explain the different jobs of DNS and HTTPS. Start with the short explanation below. Read the new-word meaning, follow one part at a time, and try the activity only when the idea makes sense. You do not need to memorize a list of tool names.

lessons.analogy: A directory gives an address; a verified identity at the door is a separate check.

steps.title: Resolve
steps.text: Use a name to identify the destination; do not confuse name resolution with service health.
steps.meaning: The system that helps turn a name into an address.
steps.example: A directory gives an address; a verified identity at the door is a separate check.

steps.title: Connect
steps.text: Choose the right address and port. Firewalls may allow or deny that path.
steps.meaning: Technology that protects a connection, used by HTTPS.
steps.example: Choose the right address and port. Firewalls may allow or deny that path.

steps.title: Protect
steps.text: HTTPS requires correctly configured certificates and a TLS endpoint.
steps.meaning: Information used to help verify the server identity for a secure connection.
steps.example: HTTPS requires correctly configured certificates and a TLS endpoint.

steps.title: Scope
steps.text: Keep this learning service local. Document a proposed boundary before exposing anything.
steps.meaning: Information used to help verify the server identity for a secure connection.
steps.example: Keep this learning service local. Document a proposed boundary before exposing anything.

lessons.commands: python labs/observability/probe.py http://127.0.0.1:8000/health

expected.en: With the local app running, one probe succeeds. This makes no claim about public DNS or TLS.

challenge.en: Write a diagram from client to TLS endpoint to private service. Label which connections are encrypted and which identity owns renewal.

quiz.question: Does DNS success prove app health?
quiz.explanation: Name resolution does not validate application behavior.

glossary.meaning: The system that helps turn a name into an address.
Technology that protects a connection, used by HTTPS.
Information used to help verify the server identity for a secure connection.

lessons.goal: Explain the different jobs of DNS and HTTPS.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete Day 8 first. If its activity is unclear, go back before adding a new tool.
lessons.takeaway: Explain the different jobs of DNS and HTTPS.
lessons.overview: DNS translates a name into addressing information; it does not guarantee the destination is healthy. TLS protects a connection and authenticates a server name through certificates. A public endpoint adds exposure and responsibility. This local service intentionally has neither TLS termination nor authentication and should not be treated as a public production API.

concept.en: Describe what one app route promises to return. Start with the short explanation below. Read the new-word meaning, follow one part at a time, and try the activity only when the idea makes sense. You do not need to memorize a list of tool names.

lessons.analogy: A menu tells customers what they can order and what to expect back.

steps.title: Read
steps.text: Find the do_GET handler and the route comparisons.
steps.meaning: A path a web app responds to, such as /health.
steps.example: A menu tells customers what they can order and what to expect back.

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: Call the home and health endpoints and inspect their different response bodies.
steps.meaning: The behavior callers can expect, such as a response status and its contents.
steps.example: Call the home and health endpoints and inspect their different response bodies.

steps.title: Configure
steps.text: APP_VERSION changes the reported version without changing source.
steps.meaning: A text format for structured data, using names and values.
steps.example: APP_VERSION changes the reported version without changing source.

steps.title: Document
steps.text: Write a small table of route, expected status and body fields.
steps.meaning: A text format for structured data, using names and values.
steps.example: Write a small table of route, expected status and body fields.

lessons.commands:
python app.py
# Second terminal:
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/missing

expected.en: Home returns message/version; health returns status; missing returns HTTP 404.

challenge.en: Suggest a new /ready route and specify its exact contract before writing code.

quiz.question: What belongs in a route contract?
quiz.explanation: Clients need predictable status and response data.

glossary.meaning: A path a web app responds to, such as /health.
The behavior callers can expect, such as a response status and its contents.
A text format for structured data, using names and values.

lessons.goal: Describe what one app route promises to return.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete Day 9 first. If its activity is unclear, go back before adding a new tool.
lessons.takeaway: Describe what one app route promises to return.
lessons.overview: A contract describes what a caller can depend on: supported routes, status codes, content type and response shape. Our service has a home response and a health endpoint; an unknown route is a 404. Configuration controls the version field. A contract lets you make changes without silently breaking clients.

title.en: Write a test that can fail

concept.en: Show a test that catches incorrect behavior. Start with the short explanation below. Read the new-word meaning, follow one part at a time, and try the activity only when the idea makes sense. You do not need to memorize a list of tool names.

lessons.analogy: A smoke detector must react to smoke, not merely confirm that its casing exists.

steps.title: Arrange
steps.text: Create the temporary server and test input.
steps.meaning: A small program that checks whether behavior matches an expectation.
steps.example: A smoke detector must react to smoke, not merely confirm that its casing exists.

steps.title: Act
steps.text: Send the HTTP request for the behavior being checked.
steps.meaning: The comparison that makes a test pass or fail.
steps.example: Send the HTTP request for the behavior being checked.

steps.title: Assert
steps.text: Compare status or body to the intended contract.
steps.meaning: Giving a predictable result when the same relevant inputs are used.
steps.example: Compare status or body to the intended contract.

steps.title: Clean
steps.text: Stop the temporary server so later tests do not inherit leaked processes.
steps.meaning: Giving a predictable result when the same relevant inputs are used.
steps.example: Stop the temporary server so later tests do not inherit leaked processes.

lessons.commands: python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

expected.en: Find test_unknown_path and explain how it would fail if the app returned 200 for every path.

challenge.en: Change the 404 route behavior in a temporary branch. Confirm the correct test fails, then restore it.

quiz.question: Which test is stronger?
options: A test that detects an incorrect response
quiz.explanation: A meaningful assertion must distinguish correct and broken behavior.

glossary.meaning: A small program that checks whether behavior matches an expectation.
The comparison that makes a test pass or fail.
Giving a predictable result when the same relevant inputs are used.

lessons.goal: Show a test that catches incorrect behavior.
lessons.prerequisite: Complete Day 10 first. If its activity is unclear, go back before adding a new tool.
lessons.takeaway: Show a test that catches incorrect behavior.
